Artificial Neural Networks → Week 5: Backpropagation and Training Dynamics → Lesson 3: Gradient Flow and Initialisation Gradient Flow and Initialisation ¶ Key Concepts ¶ 1. Why Gradient Flow Matters in Deep Networks ¶ What gradient flow is ¶ Gradients travel backward from the output layer to the first layer. This backward movement is gradient flow . ★ A layer can only learn if a usable gradient actually reaches it . Good flow: gradients reach all layers with a meaningful size and stable direction, so all layers learn together. Poor flow: gradients become extremely small or extremely large, and learning breaks down. Gradient flow is a health indicator for training . Why depth causes the problem ¶ At every layer the gradient is multiplied by a local derivative , so an early layer's gradient is a product of many numbers . Mostly < 1 → gradients shrink exponentially; mostly > 1 → they grow exponentially, with depth. This is a fundamental mathematical consequence of depth, not a software or hardware problem. The two failure modes ¶ Vanishing gradients Exploding gradients Gradient size Extremely close to 0 Extremely large Effect Early layers get almost no learning signal; training is very slow or stuck Parameter updates become unstable; training diverges numerically The earliest layers are farthest from the error , so they receive gradients after the most multiplications. Common failure mode: a deep network behaves like a shallow one , because the early layers never truly learn. Gradient flow as a diagnostic ¶ Healthy training: gradients across layers stay reasonably scaled; no layer is starved. Unhealthy: gradients collapse to 0 in early layers, or blow up unpredictably. Practitioners often monitor gradient norms across layers to catch this early. What determines health: the activation function , weight initialisation , network depth , and even numerical precision . ★ Most training failures in deep networks are ultimately gradient flow failures. What "good" means: gradients reaching early layers have a meaningful magnitude and a stable direction . If a gradient flips sign randomly between iterations the weights just hover around a point. If it is near 0, updates don't change the error; if it is huge you get infinities and numerical instability. Of the four factors, activation function, initialisation and depth matter most for network design; numerical precision is usually a fixed standard. Sigmoid/tanh example: on the flat ends of the S-curve the slope is ≈ 0, so moving a weight there barely changes the output. 2. Weight and Bias Initialisation ¶ Why it matters ¶ Training starts with the network knowing nothing: every weight and bias needs an initial value. These decide how activations and gradients scale, and whether learning starts smoothly or fails immediately. Bad initialisation can block learning completely; good initialisation makes deep networks trainable. Why not all zeros? Symmetry ¶ flowchart TD A["All weights = 0"] --> B["Every neuron in a layer gets
the same input and gives the same output"] B --> C["In backprop, every neuron gets
the same gradient"] C --> D["Neurons stay identical forever:
clones that learn the same feature"] This is the symmetry-breaking problem : weights must never be initialised to zero. Chain of effect: initial weights set the size of z₁ , which sets the size of the activation h , which sets the gradient size and so the stability of learning. With all weights 0, z₁ = z₂ = 0 : both neurons learn the same thing, so the layer's expressive power is poor. Biases are different: a bias does not multiply inputs, so it does not create symmetry. b = 0 is standard practice. (With ReLU, a small positive bias is sometimes used to avoid dead neurons, but it is optional.) What makes an initialisation good ¶ Activations should neither blow up nor collapse to 0, and gradients should keep a healthy size across layers. ★ The idea behind modern methods: preserve stable variance in both the forward and backward passes. Naive random initialisation ¶ Drawing w ~ N(0, σ²) : σ too small → weighted sums shrink, activations shrink layer by layer → vanishing gradients. σ too large → weighted sums explode → huge activations → exploding gradients. ( σ² here is the variance of the normal distribution, not the sigmoid.) Plain N(0, σ²) is acceptable for small networks (2–3 layers) but not for deeper ones. A layer computes z = Σ wᵢxᵢ ; its variance depends on the number of inputs, the input variance and the weight variance. Across many layers this keeps being multiplied, so it grows or shrinks exponentially . Analogy: a note passed down a line of singers, each making it louder or quieter. Each layer scales the signal by After 20 layers Result 0.5 (weights too small) 0.5²⁰ ≈ 10⁻⁶ Signal fades; gradients vanish 1.5 (weights too large) 1.5²⁰ ≈ 3,300 Signal blows up; gradients explode ≈ 1.0 ≈ 1 Healthy Goal of a good initialisation: each layer keeps the signal's size roughly constant , forward and backward. Why variance depends on n_in : z = w₁x₁ + … + wₙxₙ sums n terms, so more inputs give a bigger spread, so the weights must be smaller when there are more inputs . Example with He: 100 inputs → variance 2/100 = 0.02 (std ≈ 0.14); 1,000 inputs → variance 0.002. Xavier (Glorot) vs He initialisation ¶ Xavier (Glorot) He Designed for Sigmoid and tanh ReLU family Gaussian form w ~ N(0, 1/n_in) w ~ N(0, 2/n_in) Uniform form A uniform range set from n_in and n_out — Idea Keep activation and gradient variance stable across layers Factor 2 compensates for ReLU zeroing roughly half the inputs n_in = neurons feeding the layer (the previous layer); n_out = neurons in this layer. Xavier is not ideal for ReLU : ReLU zeroes about half the inputs, cutting the signal variance in half. He initialisation corrects this. Modern deep networks with ReLU and its variants almost always use He initialisation . Standard uniform form of Xavier: w ~ U(−√(6/(n_in + n_out)), +√(6/(n_in + n_out))) . The live class confirmed the bounds come from 6 / (n_in + n_out) ; the derivation is out of scope. Xavier is used for sigmoid, tanh and linear layers ; He is essentially the same idea with 1 replaced by 2 , for ReLU. Summary ¶ Zero weights break learning (symmetry), but zero bias is usually fine. Naive random initialisation often leads to vanishing or exploding gradients. Xavier → tanh/sigmoid networks; He → ReLU-family networks. Poor initialisation: immediate vanishing/exploding gradients, flat loss curves, instability or divergence. Good initialisation: smooth early learning, stable gradient flow, faster convergence. ★ It is the foundation of model training, not a tuning detail.

Artificial Neural Networks → Week 5: Backpropagation and Training Dynamics → Lesson 4: Loss Functions Loss Functions ¶ Key Concepts ¶ 1. Mean Squared Error (MSE) Loss ¶ Why a loss function ¶ A loss function turns "how wrong is this prediction?" into a single number. Backpropagation uses that number to compute gradients and update weights. Different tasks need different losses. ★ The loss supplies the starting gradient ∂E/∂ŷ for backpropagation, so its formula decides what flows backward. MSE ¶ MSE = (1/n) Σ (y − ŷ)² — take the error, square it, average it. A smooth, always non-negative measure of distance; geometrically, the squared distance between the true and predicted point. Example ¶ True y = 5 , predictions 4 and 2: (5 − 4)² = 1 , (5 − 2)² = 9 → average = 5 . ★ Squaring punishes large errors much more strongly than small ones. Order of operations: find the error, square it, then average over the batch (e.g. add up 32 squared errors and divide by 32). Error 1 → 1, but error 4 → 16: the error grew 4×, the penalty 16×. Negative errors count the same, since squares are non-negative. MSE is convex and differentiable, so it is easy to optimise. For one point, ∂E/∂ŷ = 2(ŷ − y) is the gradient that starts backpropagation. When to use it ¶ Default loss for regression (continuous outputs): house prices, temperature forecasts, sensor readings, energy consumption, autoencoders (reconstructing inputs). Poor for classification (next video). 2. Cross-Entropy and Softmax ¶ Why MSE fails for classification ¶ Problem Explanation Wrong geometry Treats class labels as numbers on a line (0, 1, 2), but class 2 is not "twice" class 1: there is no natural numeric distance between classes → poor decision boundaries Weak penalty for confident mistakes True class = 1: predicting 0.9 gives MSE 0.01; predicting 0.1 gives 0.81 — both small, so the feedback is weak Tiny gradients with sigmoid/softmax These saturate near 0 and 1, so their derivatives are tiny. With y = 1 and ŷ = 0.99 the loss is only 0.0001, and a confidently wrong model gets almost no corrective signal Softmax recap ¶ A network outputs raw scores called logits (any sign, don't sum to 1). Softmax turns them into a probability distribution: pᵢ = e^(zᵢ) / Σⱼ e^(zⱼ) . Every output is positive and all outputs sum to 1; a larger logit gets a higher probability. (The numerically stable version was covered in the maths module.) Cross-entropy ¶ For true class y : CE = −log(p_y) — how surprised the model is that the true class occurred. Probability given to the true class (cat) Loss Reading 0.90 ≈ 0.1 Almost perfect 0.50 ≈ 0.69 Unsure 0.01 ≈ 4.6 Confidently wrong: loss shoots up Message to the model: if you are confidently wrong, correct aggressively. Side-by-side, true label 1: MSE goes from 0.01 (prediction 0.9) to only 0.81 (prediction 0.1); cross-entropy goes from ≈ 0.1 to ≈ 2.3 . The much larger loss gives a usable signal when it propagates backward. Cross-entropy is just −log of the probability the model gave the true class. It is not the sigmoid ( 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ) ), though the two are related: the log-odds log(p / (1 − p)) is the inverse of sigmoid. Softmax + cross-entropy together ¶ In practice they are computed as one expression : loss = −z_y + log Σⱼ e^(zⱼ) . This avoids extra computation and is numerically stable. PyTorch and TensorFlow implement this internally: calling CrossEntropyLoss already includes the softmax . ★ Softmax + cross-entropy is the default for classification : strong, well-shaped gradients; pushes probability toward the correct class; heavily penalises confident mistakes; scales to many classes; trains faster and more reliably than MSE. Used in CNNs, RNNs, transformers and almost every modern classifier. 3. How Loss Influences Gradient Signals ¶ The loss shapes the gradients ¶ Pipeline: forward pass → loss → backpropagation → weight update. The loss is not just a measure of error: different losses give different gradient magnitudes and directions , which changes how fast and how well a model learns. MSE vs cross-entropy gradients ¶ MSE (classifier) Cross-entropy + softmax Gradient ≈ error × activation derivative ≈ p − y (predicted probability − target) Problem / benefit The activation derivative is tiny when outputs sit near 0 or 1 → dampens the signal No extra tiny multiplier; direct and larger corrections Cases ¶ Situation MSE gradient Cross-entropy gradient Unsure (p ≈ 0.5 for the true class) error 0.5 × derivative 0.25 = 0.125 (moderate) p − y = −0.5 (stronger push) Confidently wrong (p ≈ 0.01) error 0.99 × tiny derivative (≈ 0.01 at that saturation point) ≈ ~0 −0.99 (very large correction) Confident and correct Small Small (appropriate: only fine-tuning needed) ★ The key difference: cross-entropy aggressively punishes confident wrong answers ; MSE often does not, because the saturated activation derivative cancels the large error. MSE can leave a confidently wrong classifier stuck . flowchart LR A["Model confidently wrong"] --> B["MSE: large error x
tiny activation derivative"] A --> C["Cross-entropy: gradient = p − y"] B --> D["Almost no corrective signal
slow or stuck learning"] C --> E["Large corrective signal
fast correction"] Conceptual plot (gradient magnitude vs predicted probability p ): cross-entropy starts high when p is small and declines smoothly toward 0 as p rises; MSE peaks near the middle and is very small at the edges. Empirically, classifiers trained with softmax + cross-entropy converge faster and reach better performance than the same models trained with MSE. ★ Choosing the loss is a design decision that directly affects learning dynamics. Artificial Neural Networks → Week 6: Optimisation Algorithms → Lesson 2: Gradient Descent and Momentum Gradient Descent and Momentum ¶ Key Concepts ¶ 1. What is Optimisation? ¶ The goal of training ¶ Training aims to minimise the loss . Optimisation = finding the weights and biases that make the loss as small as possible. The optimiser explores combinations of parameters, trying to move the model into a region where it performs well. The loss landscape ¶ With thousands or millions of parameters, the loss is a high-dimensional surface with valleys, hills, plateaus, ridges and saddle points . There can be several local minima and one global minimum ; near a saddle point the surface is almost flat. ★ Optimisation finds a good enough valley and navigates the landscape efficiently, avoiding the regions that slow learning. Why it's hard: the surface is high-dimensional, gradients can be noisy or inconsistent, some regions are nearly flat and others very steep, and a poor learning rate can make training slow or unstable. What the optimiser controls ¶ Aspect Tool Step size Learning rate Directional smoothing Momentum Per-parameter adjustment Adaptive optimisers (RMSProp, Adam) Stability Gradient clipping , normalisation ★ Together these decide convergence speed, final accuracy and training stability. Optimisation is more than computing the gradients. 2. Gradient Descent ¶ Intuition ¶ Imagine standing on a curved landscape defined by the loss, with the parameter as a ball. Gradient descent: look at the slope and step downhill . Slope negative (loss rises to the left) → move right . Slope positive (loss rises to the right) → move left . Slope ≈ flat → near a minimum. The gradient points in the direction the loss grows fastest (uphill), so the optimiser moves in the opposite direction. Update rule ¶ θ_new = θ_old − η · ∇L θ = the weight being updated, η = learning rate , ∇L = gradient (the slope at the current point). The gradient gives the direction ; the learning rate controls how big a step . Every parameter follows the same rule. Learning rate ¶ Learning rate Effect Too small Tiny steps, training extremely slow Too large Overshoots the minimum or diverges (loss increases) Well chosen Smooth, efficient progress downhill Real networks have millions of dimensions: the gradient is a vector with a slope for every weight and bias, but the logic is unchanged: take a step that reduces the loss the most. Worked check: L(θ) = (θ − 3)² ¶ Gradient ∇L = 2(θ − 3) , start at θ = 0 . Step η = 0.1 η = 1.1 Start θ = 0, gradient −6 θ = 0, gradient −6 After 1 update θ = 0.6 (gradient −4.8) θ = 6.6 (gradient +7.2) After 2 updates θ = 1.08 (steadily approaching 3) θ = −1.32 (overshooting more each time) η = 0.1 creeps toward the minimum at 3; η = 1.1 jumps past it and the distance from 3 keeps growing (3 → 3.6 → 4.3 → …): divergence. Practical points from the live class ¶ Where this sits: backpropagation gives the gradient of the loss for every weight and bias; optimisation is the step that uses those gradients to update them . Then the next batch uses the new weights, the loss and gradients are recomputed, and the loop repeats. The loss is one number, the gradients are per parameter. The loss is computed once for the whole batch; each parameter then gets its own partial derivative (its share of the blame), e.g. W1 ← W1 − η · ∂E/∂W1 , W2 ← W2 − η · ∂E/∂W2 . It is a joint optimisation : all parameters are updated together and do not counter each other. Only the sign matters for direction: positive gradient → decrease the parameter, negative gradient → increase it. The actual weight value can be anything (−2, +10). η is a scaling factor on the gradient (typical values 0.1, 0.01, 10⁻³), not a "rate" in the physics sense; it is the size of the change in θ per update. Reaching a minimum: the slope is ≈ 0, so θ_new ≈ θ_old and updates stall. It is normal to explore a little uphill to check it is a real minimum. You often end in a good local minimum , and that is fine; you never see the true loss curve, only the path your training traces. When to stop (in practice): real loss surfaces are not smooth, and some weights may want to move in opposite directions near the end. Teams stop when the loss stops improving or when business metrics (precision, recall, ...) are good enough. One data point is enough for a gradient: the loss has a fixed functional form (e.g. (y − ŷ)² or −log ŷ ), so you can differentiate it for a single sample. That is why SGD (batch of 1) works. 3. Variants of Gradient Descent ¶ Why variants exist ¶ With millions of samples, computing one gradient over the whole dataset is slow, expensive, memory-heavy and hard to scale. The variants differ only in how much data each update uses . flowchart LR A["Batch GD

Batch size matters ¶ Batch size Behaviour Small (16, 32) Noisier gradients; can improve generalisation and escape bad regions Large (1024+) Very smooth gradients, but may converge to sharp minima and need learning-rate tuning or warm-up 32–256 Works extremely well for most tasks ★ Batch size is one of the most important hyperparameters. Noise is sometimes exactly what the optimiser needs to keep moving. Practical points from the live class ¶ Naming is confusing: "batch gradient descent" means the entire dataset per update. "Mini-batch" means whatever batch size you train with (e.g. 32). When code or slides say SGD , it almost always means mini-batch gradient descent . Mini-batches are formed by random sampling , so re-training can give a slightly different loss curve (e.g. 45 vs 60 epochs to converge). Well-represented batches give smoother curves. Batch GD is the ideal but impractical for large data; pure SGD (1 sample) suits online / real-time learning but gives a very wavy loss. 4. Momentum ¶ The problem: zig-zag ¶ In a narrow valley (steep in one direction, shallow in the one we want), the gradient keeps pointing left and right across the walls. The optimiser wastes time correcting direction and converges slowly. The idea: velocity ¶ Momentum keeps a running average of past gradients , like a ball rolling downhill: it keeps going through a gentle patch because it has accumulated speed. Gradients consistently in one direction → the update builds speed . Gradients oscillate → momentum smooths them out. Gradients very small → momentum carries the update forward. Update rule ¶ v_t = β · v_{t−1} + (1 − β) · ∇L θ_t = θ_{t−1} − η · v_t β = how much of the previous velocity to keep; typical β = 0.9 (keep 90% of the previous direction). Conceptually: a weighted average of recent gradients. flowchart LR A["Without momentum

slow progress"] B["With momentum

the valley floor"] Benefits ¶ Accelerates convergence, especially in long, narrow valleys . Reduces oscillation in steep dimensions. Helps escape shallow local minima; gives more stable training. Most useful with noisy mini-batch gradients , slow training, or narrow valleys. A standard addition to SGD; Adam includes a version of momentum internally. Practical points from the live class ¶ Reading β : β = 0.9 gives 90% weight to history and 10% to the current gradient; 1 − β is the weight on the current gradient. β lies between 0 and 1. Momentum carries across batches: v_{t−1} for the next batch is the v_t from the previous batch, so the velocity keeps accumulating through training. In the update, the velocity replaces the raw gradient ( θ ← θ − η · v_t ). Momentum helps most in deep valleys and strongly curved regions, and on flat patches. All gradient descent variants share one global learning rate η for every parameter; that is the limitation adaptive optimisers address (next lesson).

Artificial Neural Networks → Week 6: Optimisation Algorithms → Lesson 3: Adaptive Optimisers Adaptive Optimisers ¶ Key Concepts ¶ 1. Why Adaptive Methods Were Needed ¶ Limits of SGD and momentum ¶ SGD uses one global learning rate for every parameter , but parameters behave very differently: some are sensitive and need tiny steps, others barely affect the loss and need large ones. A shared rate makes some learn too slowly and others unstable. The mismatch grows as networks get deeper. Situation Problem with a single learning rate Sparse features (NLP, recommenders, sparse inputs) Many features are 0 most of the time, so their weights get rare gradients and hardly move Varying gradient size across layers Large-gradient parameters overshoot ; small-gradient ones barely move Noisy mini-batch gradients The noise adds to the mismatch Plateaus and saddle points Large rate → divergence; small rate → very slow, even with momentum What is needed: step sizes that depend on each parameter's own gradient history . The adaptive idea ¶ Adaptive optimisers compute a per-parameter learning rate from the history of the gradients: noisy parameters → dampened updates sparse parameters → boosted updates stable directions → accelerated updates Each parameter learns at the speed appropriate to it. 2. RMSProp ¶ Idea ¶ Track how large each parameter's gradients have been recently . Consistently large gradients → reduce its step size; small gradients → increase its effective step size. Each parameter gets its own dynamically adjusted step. Update rule ¶ Running average of squared gradients: E[g²]_t = β · E[g²]_{t−1} + (1 − β) · g_t² Parameter update: θ_t = θ_{t−1} − η · g_t / √(E[g²]_t + ε) The key part is the denominator : large recent gradients → large denominator → small update; small gradients → small denominator → larger update. Intuition with numbers ¶ Two weights with steady gradients of 100 and 0.01, η = 0.001 : Plain SGD: steps of 0.001 × 100 = 0.1 and 0.001 × 0.01 = 0.00001 : wildly unequal. RMSProp: each gradient is divided by roughly its own typical size, so both steps are about η = 0.001 : balanced learning. Benefits and defaults ¶ Reduces oscillation in steep directions, handles noisy mini-batch gradients, lets sparse-gradient parameters learn faster, and adjusts the rate continuously. Artificial Neural Networks → Week 6: Optimisation Algorithms → Lesson 4: Learning Rate Scheduling Learning Rate Scheduling ¶ Key Concepts ¶ 1. Why a Fixed Learning Rate Is Limiting ¶ What the learning rate does ¶ It sets how big a step the optimiser takes at every update: how fast the model learns, how stable training is, and whether it converges at all. A fixed rate assumes the same step size suits every stage of training. It rarely does. Training has phases ¶ Phase Situation Best step size Early Far from the optimum; gradients large Large steps → rapid progress Late Near a minimum; gradients small Small steps; large ones cause oscillation or prevent convergence Failure modes ¶ Learning rate What happens Too large Overshoots the minimum and bounces back and forth; loss oscillates or rises; may diverge. The loss curve refuses to go down smoothly Too small Painfully slow; tiny progress; struggles on flat regions; wastes computation (stable but impractical for large models) A fixed rate forces a bad compromise: large → fast start, poor finish; small → stable but extremely slow. ★ Fix: learning-rate scheduling — change the rate over time to match the phase: fast initial learning, smoother convergence later, better final performance. 2. Popular Learning Rate Schedules ¶ A schedule defines how the learning rate changes as training progresses: start relatively large, then gradually reduce. Schedule How it works Pros / cons Step decay Constant for a while, then drops sharply at set points, e.g. 0.1 for the first 30 epochs → 0.01 → 0.001 Simple, works well for many CNN models; you must choose when and how much to decay Exponential decay Multiply the rate by a fixed factor each step or epoch Smooth and predictable; if too aggressive, the rate gets too small too early Cosine annealing Follows a cosine curve: starts high, falls smoothly, very small near the end Smooth transitions; popular for large models; often used with warm restarts Warm-up Start with a very small rate and increase it over a few steps/epochs, then switch to a decay schedule Prevents unstable early updates; important for large batch sizes and transformers flowchart LR A["Warm-up
rate rises from very small"] --> B["Main decay
cosine annealing or step decay"] B --> C["Fine-tuning
very small rate"] In practice schedules are rarely used alone. The common pattern: short warm-up + main decay → stability at the start, fast progress in the middle, precise fine-tuning at the end. Which schedule? ¶ There is no single best schedule; it depends on the model, data and setup. Step decay — simple, works well for many CNN-based models. Exponential decay — when smooth reductions are wanted. Cosine annealing — popular in modern, large-scale deep learning. Warm-up — almost mandatory for transformers and large-batch training. ★ Scheduling almost always improves training stability and convergence. Practical points from the live class ¶ Why decay: early on the model is far from the optimum, so large steps explore the loss landscape quickly; near a minimum, large steps overshoot and oscillate around it, so you want small, fine-grained steps . Where you set it: the schedule is configured in code together with the optimiser (e.g. Adam with η = 0.1 plus a schedule). Step vs smooth schedules: all of them start high and end low. Step decay has sudden drops at chosen epochs (you must decide when and by how much); exponential and cosine follow a smooth mathematical curve , which is usually more stable and less jerky. Cosine stays high for longer before falling, and empirically often does better. Exponential decay needs careful tuning of its factor γ , or it can shrink too fast. Typical combined pattern: warm-up → main decay (cosine or step) → fixed very small rate (10⁻³ to 10⁻⁴) near convergence. Warm-up is used when early training is unstable (NaNs), with large batch sizes, and in transformers. What an "epoch" means here is flexible: the schedule can step per full pass over the data, per batch, or per group of 10–20 batches; some setups treat every batch as an "epoch". There is no single right choice. For small datasets (thousands of rows) you can use the whole dataset per update, which is more stable. Adam / RMSProp are adaptive, so they normally use fewer schedules; schedules are mostly paired with gradient descent methods. Raising the rate can also help jump out of a sharp minimum. 3. Adaptive vs Scheduled Learning Rates ¶ Two ways to control the step size ¶ Adaptive : the optimiser adjusts the step per parameter from the gradient history (RMSProp, Adam). Scheduled : you explicitly change the learning rate over time by a predefined plan (step decay, cosine annealing, warm-up). Adaptive (Adam, RMSProp) Scheduled Strengths Powerful early; handle noisy and sparse gradients; little tuning; converge quickly; robust to gradient scale differences across layers Precise control of the step size over time; improves late-stage stability and final generalisation, especially with SGD + momentum Limitations Can reach sharp minima that generalise worse; less explicit control later in training Manual design and tuning; not per parameter; sensitive to the initial rate; assumes training is already fairly stable Best when Training is difficult, noisy or exploratory Training is stable and final performance matters Common combinations ¶ flowchart TD A["Adam + fixed LR
simple, fast baseline"] --> B["Adam + LR schedule
better stability and convergence"] B --> C["Adam first, then SGD + momentum
+ LR schedule for fine-tuning
(most popular)"] ★ Combining both ideas is common and effective; no universal best choice.

Artificial Neural Networks → Week 6: Optimisation Algorithms → Lesson 5: Stability and Convergence Stability and Convergence ¶ Key Concepts ¶ 1. Gradient Clipping ¶ The problem ¶ Gradients can grow extremely large → huge parameter updates → loss spikes, unstable training, or a crash with NaN . Even one bad update can ruin an otherwise stable run. Common in recurrent networks , very deep models , and early training when parameters are poorly initialised. The idea ¶ A safety mechanism : before applying an update, check the gradient size. Within a reasonable range → unchanged. Too large → scale it down . No single update can be catastrophically large. It limits update magnitude without changing the overall optimisation process. flowchart LR A["Compute gradient"] --> B{"Too large?"} B -->|"No"| C["Use as is"] B -->|"Yes"| D["Scale it down"] C --> E["Apply update"] D --> E Two types ¶ Clipping by value Clipping by norm How Limits each gradient component to a fixed range Scales the whole gradient vector if its norm exceeds a threshold Direction Can distort the direction Preserves the direction, limits the magnitude Use Simple More common Example (clip by norm, threshold 5): gradient (30, 40) has norm 50 → scaled by 5/50 to (3, 4) , which points the same way. When to use it ¶ Training recurrent models , very deep networks , or using large learning rates ; sudden loss spikes or exploding gradients early in training. Well-behaved models may not need it at all. What it does not do ¶ Doesn't improve generalisation, doesn't fix vanishing gradients, and doesn't replace good learning-rate choices or initialisation. ★ A safeguard, not a replacement for good optimisation. Practical points from the live class ¶ NaN in the loss means training is broken: stop and change something (architecture, initialisation, learning rate, clipping). It usually shows up in the first 5–10 epochs if it is going to happen. Why ReLU-family networks: ReLU is unbounded for positive inputs, so exploding gradients are common in ReLU-based RNNs, LSTMs and transformers, which is where clipping is standard. Clipping gives you control over how far values may grow (unlike saturating activations, which cap them automatically and cause vanishing gradients). Clipping by value: any gradient above the threshold τ is set to τ . By norm: compute the magnitude of the whole gradient vector and, if it exceeds τ , scale all components down proportionally. Update equation view: θ ← θ − η · ∇L . Clipping controls the gradient term; learning-rate schedules control the η term. A large η or large gradients both call for clipping, so it is a balance. Clipping is one of several fixes (lower the learning rate, better initialisation, normalisation), not the only one. Normalisation (recap from the live class) ¶ Batch norm normalises each feature using the mean and standard deviation across the batch ; layer norm normalises across the features of one sample . Both keep activation magnitudes under control, which helps against exploding gradients. Batch norm is the usual default; transformers prefer layer norm because attention works per sample and parallelises across features. Batch norm is a poor fit for time series with seasonality that is not present in every batch. The four stabilisers: proper initialisation (Xavier / He), better activations (ReLU family), gradient clipping , normalisation layers . 2. Optimisation Pitfalls ¶ Training doesn't always explode: it often starts normally, then slows, stalls or fluctuates . These are frequently optimisation challenges, not code or data bugs. Pitfall What it is Effect Saddle points Gradient ≈ 0 but not a minimum (shaped like a horse saddle: up in one direction, down in another) Far more common than local minima in high dimensions; the optimiser gets stuck or very slow, so it looks converged when it hasn't Plateaus Extremely flat regions; tiny gradients Progress very slow; common in deep networks and with saturating activations Noisy updates Mini-batch randomness Helps escape saddle points, but makes the loss fluctuate and harder to interpret Poor conditioning Very different curvature in different directions (some steep, some flat) Zig-zag updates, slow progress, high sensitivity to learning rate. Helped by momentum, adaptive optimisers, normalisation Optimisation problem or modelling problem? ¶ flowchart TD A["Training problem"] --> B{"Does the loss decrease?"} B -->|"No, or erratic"| C["Optimisation issue
fix training dynamics"] B -->|"Yes, but performance is poor"| D["Model capacity or data issue"] Responses to optimisation issues: adjust the learning rate , switch optimisers , add momentum or gradient clipping , improve the initialisation . These target training dynamics, not the architecture. ★ Diagnosing these issues is an essential skill. 3. Convergence Behaviour: Noisy vs Smooth Descent ¶ What convergence looks like ¶ Expect the loss to decrease and updates to get smaller, but it doesn't always look smooth. Smooth convergence Noisy convergence Typical cause Large batches , gradients averaged over many samples Mini-batches , small batch sizes, relatively high learning rates Loss curve Steady, minimal fluctuation, easy to interpret Goes up and down while the overall trend is downward Downsides Can be slower; may reach sharper minima that generalise worse Harder to interpret Upsides Predictable Helps escape saddle points and poor regions; encourages exploration; often finds flatter minima , which generalise better ★ Noisy descent is normal and often beneficial; smooth descent is easier to read but not always better. Batch size and optimiser effects ¶ Small batches : more noise and exploration, curves harder to read. Large batches : less noise, smoother curves, less exploration, possibly poorer generalisation. No single best batch size. SGD with momentum : tends to be noisier but often generalises well . Adam / RMSProp : usually smoother early training and faster convergence, but may settle into sharper minima . How to read training curves ¶ Focus on the long-term trend : is the loss decreasing overall? Does the noise shrink over time? Does validation performance improve? Don't react to short-term fluctuations; they are a normal part of training. Practical points from the live class ¶ Saddle points are escaped by noise only if the step is big enough: the gradient there is tiny, so a small learning rate or large batch will not jump out; a higher rate or smaller batch can. Momentum helps but may not be enough, so even Adam can get stuck. Stalled convergence can come from saddle points, plateaus, noise or poor conditioning. Smoother curve = larger batch + smaller learning rate , at the cost of slower convergence and a risk of settling in a sharp minimum that is hard to leave. Noisy descent (small batches, higher rate, diverse data) often generalises better . Noise in the loss curve ≠ noisy data. Diversity in the data adds to loss fluctuation, but don't clean it away: it may be real signal. With large datasets deep models cope; with small datasets be careful. Fixes to try when convergence is poor: adjust the learning rate or schedule first, then change the optimiser, add momentum or clipping, change the initialisation, raise the batch size. Judging convergence: look at the loss curve first , and only then dig into gradients per layer or parameter. The trend should go down, noise should shrink, and training and validation loss should both fall . If training loss falls while validation loss rises, that is overfitting (next topic: generalisation and regularisation). Data splits: training and validation are evaluated every epoch; the test set is a hold-out used once, after training. Debugging gradients in code is covered in modules 10–12.

3. Convergence Behaviour: Noisy vs Smooth Descent

docs.text: Expect the loss to decrease and updates to get smaller, but it doesn't always look smooth. Smooth convergence Noisy convergence Typical cause Large batches , gradients averaged over many samples Mini-batches , small batch sizes, relatively high learning rates Loss curve Steady, minimal fluctuation, easy to interpret Goes up and down while the overall trend is downward Downsides Can be slower; may reach sharper minima that generalise worse Harder to interpret Upsides Predictable Helps escape saddle points and poor regions; encourages exploration; often finds flatter minima , which generalise better ★ Noisy descent is normal and often beneficial; smooth descent is easier to read but not always better.
docs.title: What convergence looks like

docs.text: Small batches : more noise and exploration, curves harder to read. Large batches : less noise, smoother curves, less exploration, possibly poorer generalisation. No single best batch size. SGD with momentum : tends to be noisier but often generalises well . Adam / RMSProp : usually smoother early training and faster convergence, but may settle into sharper minima .
docs.title: Batch size and optimiser effects

docs.text: Focus on the long-term trend : is the loss decreasing overall? Does the noise shrink over time? Does validation performance improve? Don't react to short-term fluctuations; they are a normal part of training.
docs.title: How to read training curves

docs.text: Saddle points are escaped by noise only if the step is big enough: the gradient there is tiny, so a small learning rate or large batch will not jump out; a higher rate or smaller batch can. Momentum helps but may not be enough, so even Adam can get stuck. Stalled convergence can come from saddle points, plateaus, noise or poor conditioning. Smoother curve = larger batch + smaller learning rate , at the cost of slower convergence and a risk of settling in a sharp minimum that is hard to leave. Noisy descent (small batches, higher rate, diverse data) often generalises better . Noise in the loss curve ≠ noisy data. Diversity in the data adds to loss fluctuation, but don't clean it away: it may be real signal. With large datasets deep models cope; with small datasets be careful. Fixes to try when convergence is poor: adjust the learning rate or schedule first, then change the optimiser, add momentum or clipping, change the initialisation, raise the batch size. Judging convergence: look at the loss curve first , and only then dig into gradients per layer or parameter. The trend should go down, noise should shrink, and training and validation loss should both fall . If training loss falls while validation loss rises, that is overfitting (next topic: generalisation and regularisation). Data splits: training and validation are evaluated every epoch; the test set is a hold-out used once, after training. Debugging gradients in code is covered in modules 10–12.

Machine Learning → Week 1: Introduction to Machine Learning → Lesson 1: Machine Learning Paradigms and Workflow Machine Learning Paradigms and Workflow ¶ Summary ¶ Machine Learning emerged because digitizing everyday physical experience generated huge volumes of data, creating a need to extract patterns and knowledge from it. This lecture traces that shift through four historical paradigms of discovery, defines ML, and introduces two standard workflows for turning raw data into knowledge (KDD and CRISP-DM), plus a business-intelligence view of the same journey. It then zooms into supervised learning — learning from labelled data — covering its two flavors (classification and regression) and the training/validation/test workflow used to build and evaluate a model. It then covers unsupervised learning — finding hidden patterns in unlabelled data — through its two main tasks, clustering and association rule mining. Finally, it covers practical considerations — real-world challenges (scalability, dimensionality, data quality, and more) that a machine learning pipeline needs to handle beyond the core algorithms. Key Concepts ¶ 1. Foundations of Machine Learning ¶ Why Machine Learning emerged ¶ Physical, real-world experiences are increasingly captured as digital data (sensors, transactions, clicks, images, etc.). This digitization → massive volumes of generated data. Volume alone isn't useful — the value is in finding patterns and extracting knowledge from that data, which is what ML/data science does. The four paradigms of scientific discovery ¶ Each era added a new way of generating knowledge, building on the previous one rather than replacing it. timeline title Paradigms of Discovery Before 1600 : Empirical Science : knowledge from direct observation of the world 1600 - 1950 : Theoretical Science : knowledge from models and generalizing observations into laws/theories 1950 - 1990 : Computer Science : knowledge from running simulations of models too complex to solve analytically 1990 - Now : Data Science / ML : knowledge from uncovering patterns in massive, real-world datasets, often without a hand-built theoretical model first Definition of Machine Learning ¶ The field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed. Contrast with classical programming: instead of hand-coding rules, the system infers rules/patterns from data. KDD (Knowledge Discovery in Databases) ¶ The classic pipeline for going from raw data to actionable knowledge. flowchart LR A[Databases
raw data] --> B[Data Integration] B --> C[Data Cleaning] C --> D[Data Warehouse] D --> E[Selection
task-relevant data] E --> F[Data Mining] F --> G[Pattern Evaluation] G --> H[Knowledge] Each stage narrows and refines the data until only task-relevant, validated patterns remain as "knowledge." Data Mining here is the pattern-extraction step, not the whole pipeline. CRISP-DM (Cross Industry Standard Process for Data Mining) ¶ The most widely used industry framework for data mining/ML projects — organizes the same idea as KDD around 5 phases. flowchart TD A[Business Understanding] --> C[Prepare Data] B[Data Understanding] --> C C --> D[Building Model
using Algorithms] T[Training Data] --> D D --> E["Applying Model &
Performance Evaluation"] Te[Test Data] --> E E --> F[Deployment] F --> G[Knowledge and Actions] Phase Stage(s) What happens 1. Prior Knowledge Business Understanding, Data Understanding Understand the problem and the data available before touching a model 2. Preparation Prepare Data Clean/transform data into a usable form 3. Modeling Building Model using Algorithms Train models using training data 4. Application Applying Model and Performance Evaluation Evaluate the model against test data 5. Knowledge Deployment → Knowledge and Actions Deploy the model and act on what it produces Why it matters: gives teams a repeatable, industry-standard checklist so an ML project doesn't skip straight from data to model without understanding the business problem first. The Business Intelligence (BI) view ¶ Same overall journey (data → decisions) but framed by who does each step and how much value each layer adds — shown as a pyramid, increasing potential to support business decisions as you go up. flowchart TD A["Data Sources (DBA)
raw data from files, web, DBs"] --> B["Data Exploration (Data Analyst)
statistical summary, querying & reporting"] B --> C["Data Mining (Data Analyst)
information discovery / discovering new information"] C --> D["Data Presentation (Business Analyst)
visualization techniques"] D --> E["Decision Making (End User)
using insights to make business decisions"] Why it matters: connects the technical pipeline (KDD/CRISP-DM) to organizational roles — a DBA, data analyst, business analyst, and end user each own a layer, and value/decision-support potential increases as data moves up the pyramid. Types of data used in ML ¶ Structured — fits a fixed schema (e.g. relational tables). Unstructured — no fixed schema (e.g. free text, images). Time-variant data — values change over time. Advanced/specialized data types: Data stream & sensor data — continuous, high-velocity data from sensors/IoT. Time series & sequence data — ordered observations over time. How machines learn: prediction vs. description ¶ Two fundamental approaches to machine learning, split by whether the "correct answer" is known in advance. Supervised Learning ¶ Definition and types ¶ Definition: learning from labelled data — each training example has a known correct answer, called a class label . Complex & heterogeneous data — data arrives from various sources and mixed types (audio, video, sensors); the pipeline should handle this complexity effectively and efficiently. Data quality — noise, inconsistencies, and missing values are common; the pipeline should handle these data quality issues. Data ownership & distribution — sharing and integrating data from different sources raises both political and technical challenges that the pipeline should handle. Privacy preservation — PII must be stored ethically and legally in a protected environment (e.g. in line with GDPR). docs.text: Machine Learning emerged because digitizing everyday physical experience generated huge volumes of data, creating a need to extract patterns and knowledge from it. This lecture traces that shift through four historical paradigms of discovery, defines ML, and introduces two standard workflows for turning raw data into knowledge (KDD and CRISP-DM), plus a business-intelligence view of the same journey. It then zooms into supervised learning — learning from labelled data — covering its two flavors (classification and regression) and the training/validation/test workflow used to build and evaluate a model. It then covers unsupervised learning — finding hidden patterns in unlabelled data — through its two main tasks, clustering and association rule mining. Finally, it covers practical considerations — real-world challenges (scalability, dimensionality, data quality, and more) that a machine learning pipeline needs to handle beyond the core algorithms.

Machine Learning → Week 2: Data Preprocessing → Lesson 1: Data Fundamentals and Preprocessing Data Fundamentals and Preprocessing ¶ Key Concepts ¶ 1. Data Objects, Attributes, and Types ¶ Dataset, data objects, and attributes ¶ A dataset is a structured collection of data objects (e.g. a bank passbook: one row per transaction, with date, transaction ID, credit, debit, balance as columns). In a table, rows are data objects and columns are attributes. Data object — also called record, point, case, sample, entity, instance, tuple. Attribute — a property/characteristic of an object; also called feature, variable, field. Attribute value — the specific number or symbol an attribute takes for one object (e.g. Marital Status has values Single / Married / Divorced). A collection of attribute values together describes one object. Attribute types ¶ flowchart TD A["Attributes"] --> B["Qualitative
(categorical) — measures a quality"] A --> C["Quantitative
(numerical) — measures a quantity"] B --> D["Nominal"] B --> E["Ordinal"] C --> F["Interval"] C --> G["Ratio"] Type Meaning Examples Operations that make sense Nominal Labels that only distinguish one value from another ID number, eye colour, zip code = , ≠ (distinctness) Ordinal Values can be ranked; distance between values has no meaning Grades (A > B > C), rank, height as tall/medium/short distinctness + order ( < , > ) Interval Differences are meaningful, fixed unit, no true zero Calendar dates, temperature (°C) distinctness, order, + , − Ratio Differences and ratios are meaningful, has a true zero Length, time, count all of the above + × , ÷ Each type adds one more allowed operation on top of the previous one — ★ this decides which statistics/algorithms are valid for an attribute. Ratio makes sense because of the true zero: 10 km is twice 5 km. (20 °C is not twice 10 °C, since 0 °C isn't "no temperature".) Discrete vs continuous attributes ¶ Discrete — finite/countable set of values (zip code, binary 0/1 with cardinality 2). Continuous — infinitely many possible values (temperature: 10, 10.1, 10.11, ...). 2. Dataset Formats ¶ Why structure matters ¶ ★ The structure of a dataset determines which questions you can ask and which analysis tools you can apply. Choosing the right representation is a critical early step. flowchart TD A["Dataset formats"] --> B["Record data
fixed set of attributes per record"] A --> C["Graph data
objects + relationships"] A --> D["Ordered data
order of objects matters"] B --> B1["Data matrix"] B --> B2["Document data"] B --> B3["Transactional data"] C --> C1["Web links / social networks"] C --> C2["Molecular structures"] D --> D1["Genome sequences"] D --> D2["Spatio-temporal data"] Record data ¶ A collection of records, each with a fixed set of attributes (tabular data). Three special cases: Data matrix — all attributes numerical, so each object is a point in multi-dimensional space. Document data — each document is a term vector : every distinct term in the collection is an attribute, and the value is how often it appears (e.g. "team" 3 times, "coach" 0 times). Results in a very sparse matrix. Transactional data — each record is a set of items bought together (e.g. TID 1 → {bread, coke, milk}); attributes are not fixed per record. Graph data ¶ Used when the relationships between objects matter more than their attributes. Web: nodes = pages, edges = hyperlinks. Analysing this graph powers Google's PageRank (shows pages in descending order of importance). Chemistry: nodes = atoms, edges = chemical bonds. Ordered data ¶ Objects form a sequence where order matters (A, then B, then C...). Examples: genome sequences, transaction sequences; spatio-temporal data carries both location and time. 3. Data Quality Issues ¶ Ideal vs real world ¶ Ideal assumption: data is perfect, complete, ready for modelling. Reality: raw data is messy, incomplete, and inconsistent . ★ Garbage in, garbage out — poor-quality data → poor-quality model, whether predictive or descriptive. What is data quality? ¶ Data quality = the overall utility of a dataset for its intended purpose . Data has quality if it satisfies the requirements of the intended user — it is subjective . Same Amazon dataset can be good for an R&D manager (questions about product innovation) but poor for a delivery manager (questions about on-time delivery). Example: a credit-card fraud detector needs thousands of labelled transactions; without labels the data is poor quality for that purpose. Dimensions of data quality ¶ Dimension Question it asks Example of failure Accuracy Is the data correct? Customer name misspelled Completeness Is everything needed present? Address field half-empty Consistency Does the data contradict itself? Age doesn't match date of birth Timeliness Is it up to date? Outdated current address Believability How much can we trust it? — Interpretability Can people easily understand it? — Common data quality problems ¶ flowchart TD A["Data quality problems"] --> B["Noise"] A --> C["Outliers"] A --> D["Missing values"] A --> E["Duplicate data"] A --> F["Inconsistent values"] Noise — random error/variance added to the true value (like static on a phone line). Causes: faulty sensors, transmission problems, data-entry mistakes (e.g. census forms digitised by hand, or wrong answers given deliberately). Outliers — ★ legitimate objects whose characteristics differ considerably from most of the data. Noise is an error; an outlier is extreme but real. As a nuisance: distorts statistics. For 1, 2, 3, 4, 100 the mean is 22 ; without the outlier it is 2.5 . As the goal: the point of the analysis is to find them — credit-card fraud detection, network intrusion detection. Missing values — information not collected, attribute not applicable, or equipment malfunction. Duplicate data — duplicate/near-duplicate objects or attributes, typically after merging multiple sources. Inconsistent values — contradictions within or across records. Data preprocessing as the solution ¶ Poor data → bad business decisions, reduced trust in the system, wasted time/resources. Data preprocessing = steps applied to raw data to prepare it for later analysis. Two goals: Improve data quality — handle noise, missing values, inconsistencies. Make data fit the model — structure it so the ML/mining algorithm works well. 4. Data Preprocessing Techniques ¶ Preprocessing is a set of tasks , not a single action. Four major groups: flowchart LR A["Raw, messy data"] --> B["Data cleaning"] B --> C["Data integration"] C --> D["Data transformation"] D --> E["Data reduction"] E --> F["High-quality data
ready for modelling"] Data cleaning ¶ Fixes the quality issues from the previous section. Handling missing values flowchart TD A["Missing value"] --> B["Ignore the tuple"] A --> C["Fill manually
(tedious, infeasible at scale)"] A --> D["Fill with a global constant"] A --> E["Fill with a local constant
(per group of tuples)"] A --> F["Fill with central tendency
(mean / median)"] A --> G["Fill using a rule
(if A = 1 then B = 2)"] A --> H["Predict with a model"] Handling noisy data - Binning (local smoothing) — sort values, partition into equal-size bins, then replace each value in a bin with the bin's mean, median, or boundary value. - Regression — fit a regression function; the fitted line represents the smoothed data. - Outlier analysis — cluster the data; points falling outside the clusters are potential noise, to be handled separately. Data integration ¶ Merging data from multiple sources — must be done carefully. Typical problems: Entity identification — matching the same attribute/entity across sources. Data value conflicts — same person recorded as "John Smith" in one table and "J.D. Smith" in another. Redundancy — blind merging duplicates attributes/tuples. Example: India's voter ID, passport, driving licence, etc. were considered for merging into one master table to identify every citizen uniquely. Entity-identification, value-conflict and redundancy issues made it impractical, so Aadhaar was built from scratch instead. ★ Integration is tedious and time-consuming. Data transformation ¶ Changes the scale and structure of data to suit the algorithm — it is not about fixing errors. Normalisation — stops attributes with large magnitudes from dominating distance-based calculations (e.g. income in lakhs swamps age 1–100 in Euclidean distance) and speeds up training. Min-max normalisation Z-score normalisation Based on minimum and maximum mean and standard deviation Result values mapped linearly to a new range values centred on 0, in units of std dev Formula v' = (v − min) / (max − min) × (new_max − new_min) + new_min v' = (v − mean) / std_dev Aggregation — roll data up to a coarser level (city → state → country, quarterly → yearly). Reduces data volume, changes scale, and gives more stable data with less variability. Data reduction ¶ Goal: a much smaller representation that keeps the integrity of the original, so model building is faster and feasible. Reduce columns, rows, or both. flowchart TD A["Data reduction"] --> B["Dimensionality reduction
(fewer attributes)"] A --> C["Numerosity reduction
(fewer objects)"] B --> B1["Remove irrelevant attributes
e.g. student ID for predicting GPA"] B --> B2["Remove redundant attributes
carry the same information"] B --> B3["Attribute subset selection
forward selection, backward elimination,
decision-tree induction"] C --> C1["Histograms"] C --> C2["Clustering"] C --> C3["Sampling
simple random with / without replacement,
stratified"] Forward selection — start with an empty attribute set, add attributes one at a time, tracking performance; keep the best subset. Backward elimination works the other way, starting from all attributes. Sampling — use a representative sample that behaves almost like the full dataset.
